stem: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to recent onset of vomiting, irritability, and jaundice.  He had previously been healthy and was exclusively breastfed until a week ago, when cereals and fruit were introduced into his diet.  Physical examination shows scleral icterus and hepatomegaly.  Laboratory studies show elevated serum aminotransferase levels.  Which of the following enzymes is most likely to be deficient?​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​
explanation:
Dietary fructose is obtained mainly from fruits, vegetables, honey, table sugar (sucrose), and processed foods.  Fructose is rapidly absorbed in the proximal small bowel by the hexose transporter GLUT5.  Metabolism of fructose involves a few key enzymes, including fructokinase and aldolase B.  Fructose is initially phosphorylated by hepatic fructokinase, yielding fructose-1-phosphate.  Fructose 1-phosphate is further metabolized by aldolase B to generate dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde.  DHAP and glyceraldehyde can both be converted to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, an intermediate of glycolysis.

Aldolase B deficiency causes a potentially life-threatening disorder known as hereditary fructose intolerance.  Lack of aldolase B causes phosphorylated fructose to be trapped within the cell, depleting inorganic phosphate.  This inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, causing hypoglycemia.  This disease typically presents in infancy when fructose-containing foods are introduced into the diet, usually with vomiting after fructose ingestion.  Failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, and jaundice can also occur.  Undiagnosed individuals may eventually develop liver and renal failure.  Elimination of dietary fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol (which is metabolized to fructose) is the mainstay of treatment and results in symptom improvement with a good long-term prognosis.

(Choice A)  Most glycogen degradation occurs in the cytosol via glycogen phosphorylase and debranching enzyme; a small fraction of glycogen is degraded within lysosomes by acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase).  Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causes Pompe disease, which classically presents in infancy with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia rather than hypoglycemia.

(Choice C)  Deficiency of fructokinase causes essential fructosuria, a benign autosomal recessive disorder.  In these patients, ingested fructose is absorbed and excreted unchanged in the urine due to impairment of the first step in fructose metabolism.

(Choices D and E)  Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency (classic galactosemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by vomiting, feeding intolerance, neonatal jaundice, hepatomegaly.  In contrast to hereditary fructose intolerance, the symptoms in galactosemia start soon after breastfeeding is initiated.  Galactokinase deficiency is a more benign disorder of galactose metabolism that causes neonatal cataracts.

Educational objective:Aldolase B deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance.  Accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate depletes intracellular phosphate, impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and causing hypoglycemia after fructose ingestion.  Symptoms typically begin in infancy when fructose-containing foods are introduced and can include vomiting, failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, and jaundice.​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​
